facts.summary: Illinois requires overtime at 1.5x after 40 hours in a workweek and has no daily overtime rule, mirroring the federal FLSA standard.
facts.notes: Illinois follows the federal 40-hour weekly threshold; no state daily overtime. Illinois applies its own exemption rules under the Minimum Wage Law in addition to federal FLSA exemptions.

facts.summary: Illinois's minimum wage is $15.00 per hour for workers 18 and older, well above the federal $7.25.
facts.notes: Rate reached $15.00 on Jan 1, 2025 and remains in effect for 2026 per IDOL. Tipped minimum is $9.00/hr and youth (under 18, under 650 hrs/yr) is $13.00/hr. Some localities (e.g., Chicago, Cook County) set higher rates.

facts.summary: The Illinois Human Rights Act protects several classes beyond the federal set, including sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status, ancestry, military status, arrest/conviction record, citizenship/work authorization status, and order of protection status.
facts.sourceAgency: Illinois Human Rights Commission / Illinois Department of Human Rights
facts.notes: Listed classes are those beyond the federal baseline (race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age 40+, disability, pregnancy, genetic info). Some listed classes apply in specific contexts (e.g., source of income primarily in housing/real estate). Verify context-specific applicability against 775 ILCS 5.

facts.summary: The Illinois Human Rights Act covers employers with 1 or more employees, far broader than the federal 15-employee threshold under Title VII/ADA.
facts.notes: Effective July 1, 2020 the Act's employer definition was broadened to 1+ employee for most purposes; certain provisions (e.g., some disability accommodation counts) may have had prior thresholds. Verify exact subsection wording.

facts.value: mandatory unless prohibitively expensive or unduly disruptive
facts.summary: The Illinois Human Rights Act requires employers to make reasonable accommodation of the known physical or mental limitations of an otherwise-qualified applicant or employee with a disability -- such as facility alterations, modified schedules or leave, equipment, job restructuring, or readers/interpreters -- unless the employer can show the accommodation would be prohibitively expensive or would unduly disrupt the ordinary conduct of business.
facts.notes: IHRA's undue-hardship standard uses different wording than the ADA's ('prohibitively expensive' / 'unduly disrupt the ordinary conduct of business' rather than 'undue hardship'), confirmed via multiple independent secondary legal sources quoting the statute; the primary text at ilga.gov's statute-search tool blocks automated fetch (403), so it was not independently re-confirmed word-for-word this session -- verify directly on ilga.gov if possible. It is the employee's responsibility to request the accommodation; coverage follows the IHRA's 1+-employee threshold (see discrimination.coverage, above).

facts.summary: Illinois's Whistleblower Act bars employers from retaliating against employees who disclose (or refuse to participate in) activity they reasonably believe violates a state or federal law, rule, or regulation or poses a danger to public health or safety.
facts.notes: Act was substantially amended effective Jan 1, 2025, broadening protected disclosures and defining 'adverse employment action.' Additional anti-retaliation provisions exist in the Minimum Wage Law and Wage Payment and Collection Act.

facts.summary: A wage or final-compensation claim must be filed with the Illinois Department of Labor within one year after the wages became due.
facts.notes: One-year deadline applies to administrative claims filed with IDOL under the Wage Payment and Collection Act. A separate 10-year limitations period generally applies to private civil suits on written contracts (735 ILCS 5/13-206); verify if civil-suit deadline is needed.

facts.summary: A discrimination charge for employment (and most non-housing contexts) must be filed with the Illinois Department of Human Rights within 2 years of the alleged violation.
facts.notes: Extended from 300 days to 2 years effective Jan 1, 2025 (Public Act 103-0973). Housing violations remain 1 year. Longer than the federal EEOC 180/300-day deadlines.

facts.summary: The Illinois Freedom to Work Act voids non-compete agreements with lower-paid workers: an employer may not enter into a covenant not to compete unless the employee's actual or expected annualized earnings exceed $75,000/year (rising to $80,000 in 2027, $85,000 in 2032, $90,000 in 2037), and may not enter into a covenant not to solicit unless earnings exceed $45,000/year (rising on the same schedule to $47,500, $50,000, $52,500). A covenant entered into in violation is void and unenforceable, and non-competes are banned outright for construction-industry employees covered by a collective bargaining agreement and for many healthcare/other statutorily exempted workers.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against primary statute text (820 ILCS 90/10(a)-(b)). The Act (as amended, Public Act 102-358, eff. Jan 1, 2022) also requires 14 days' advance notice before signing and advises the employee to consult an attorney; a prevailing employee recovers costs and reasonable attorney fees from an employer who sues to enforce a void covenant.

facts.summary: Illinois requires an employer to pay a separated employee's final compensation in full at the time of separation if possible, but no later than the next regularly scheduled payday.
facts.notes: Final compensation includes earned wages, salary, commissions, bonuses, and the monetary equivalent of earned but unused vacation. Applies regardless of whether separation is voluntary or involuntary.
